title: Supreme Court Rejects Plea Seeking Maintenance Of Police Database On Persons Making Repeated Sexual Offense Complaints
summary: The Supreme Court today refused to entertain a plea seeking a structured database of complainants who lodge multiple sexual-offence cases. Underlining the need to protect identity of victims/complainants, as well as referring to existing identification mechanisms, the Court dismissed the plea.

note.Facts: A petitioners’ PIL sought a structured police database of complainants filing multiple sexual-offence complaints; the Delhi High Court had directed the police to consider the request, and the petitioners approached the Supreme Court.
note.Issue: Whether a police-maintained database of identities of complainants in sexual-offence cases should be created.
note.Held: The Supreme Court dismissed the plea, refusing to order such a database.
note.Principle: The Court held that existing two-layer identification mechanisms—mandatory medical examination with DNA profiling and recording of the victim’s statement before a Magistrate—already safeguard victim identity, and creating a police database would risk disclosure and is unnecessary.
note.Exam angle: Could be asked under the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act/IPC on sexual offences – focusing on victim-identity protection and the adequacy of existing procedural safeguards versus proposed police databases.

title: UP Urban Tenancy Act 2021 | Pending Petitions Shouldn't Be Dismissed : Supreme Court To Examine HC Verdict Striking Down Law
summary: The Supreme Court on Friday issued notice on a special leave petition against the Allahabad High Court's August ruling that struck down key provisions of the Uttar Pradesh Regulation of Urban .

note.Facts: The Allahabad High Court struck down Sections 8, 9, 10, 38 and 42 of the Uttar Pradesh Regulation of Urban Premises Tenancy Act, 2021, declaring them ultra vires and quashing an eviction order passed under the Act; the Supreme Court has issued notice on a Special Leave Petition and stayed dismissal of pending proceedings under the Act during the SLP.
note.Issue: Whether pending proceedings under the impugned provisions of the UP Regulation of Urban Premises Tenancy Act, 2021 can be dismissed as non-maintainable in view of the High Court’s declaration of those provisions as unconstitutional.
note.Held: The Supreme Court directed that, pending the SLP, proceedings under the relevant provisions of the 2021 Act shall not be dismissed as non-maintainable or abated.
note.Principle: A declaration of unconstitutionality of statutory provisions does not automatically render all pending proceedings under those provisions non-maintainable; they may continue until the higher court’s final decision on the validity of the provisions.
note.Provisions: Sections 8, 9, 10, 38, 42 (U.P. Act No 16 of 2021); Section 21(2) (U.P. Act); Article 254(2) of the Constitution; Transfer of Property Act 1882; Provincial Small Causes Courts Act 1887; 1972 Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act.
note.Exam angle: UP Regulation of Urban Premises Tenancy Act 2021 – test on repugnancy under Article 254(2) with the Transfer of Property Act 1882 and the Provincial Small Causes Courts Act 1887; focus on validity of State legislation without Presidential assent and the effect of a High Court’s striking-down on pending proceedings.

title: Supreme Court Awards Rs 10 Lakh Each To Two School Clerks For Wrongful Dismissal, Notes Poor Drafting Defeated Their Claim In HC
summary: The Supreme Court recently directed a private school to pay Rs 10 Lakh each to two clerks as compensation for the wrongful termination of their services, noting that their case had failed in the High Court because of poor drafting of the writ petitions.

note.Facts: Two clerks of a private school were terminated after an inquiry (under the Maharashtra Employees of Private Schools (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1981) in which they did not participate and were not furnished the inquiry reports. The School Tribunal stayed the termination but later dismissed their appeals, and the High Court dismissed their writ petitions under Article 226, holding they were not on the same footing as the headmaster.
note.Issue: Whether the Supreme Court can award compensation for wrongful termination despite the appellants’ poorly drafted writ petitions and the High Court’s dismissal.
note.Held: The Supreme Court exercised its power under Article 142 and directed the school to pay Rs 10 lakh each to the two clerks as lump-sum compensation for wrongful termination.
note.Principle: A party must plead all material averments in a writ petition; a court is not bound to entertain matters not pleaded. However, an order wholly contrary to an express judicial order is a nullity, and the Supreme Court may intervene under Article 142 to grant appropriate relief.
note.Provisions: Article 226, Article 142 of the Constitution; *Ram Saran Varshney v. State of U.P.* (cited). No specific statutory sections or rules are stated beyond the reference to the Maharashtra Employees of Private Schools (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1981.
note.Exam angle: Service-law question under the Maharashtra Employees of Private Schools Rules and constitutional remedies – could be asked on the scope of Article 226 vs. Article 142, or on the requirement of proper pleading in writ petitions.

title: Mere use of company’s name on counterfeit goods does not constitute copyright infringement; Bombay HC quashes FIR in JSW Steel case
summary: Bombay High Court: While examining whether the sale of counterfeit tin sheets bearing the name of JSW Steel Ltd. amounts to copyright infringement under Sections 51 and 63 of the Copyright Act, 1957 , the Single Judge Bench of M. W.

note.Facts: Counterfeit tin sheets bearing the name “JSW Steel Ltd.” were sold, and an FIR was filed alleging copyright infringement.
note.Issue: Whether the mere use of a company’s name on counterfeit goods amounts to infringement under Sections 51 and 63 of the Copyright Act, 1957.
note.Held: The Bombay High Court quashed the FIR, holding that such use does not constitute copyright infringement.
note.Principle: Use of a company’s name on counterfeit goods, without allegation of copying a copyright-protected artistic work or logo, falls outside the scope of copyright infringement and is instead a matter for trademark law.
note.Provisions: Sections 51, 63 of the Copyright Act, 1957; Section 104 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999; Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.
note.Exam angle: Test on the Copyright Act – distinction between copyright infringement and trademark infringement; could be asked to frame the issue or to list the ingredients for establishing infringement under Sections 51/63.

title: Marriage Between Hindu And Christian Can't Be Validated By Registration Under Hindu Marriage Act: Madras High Court
ratio: The marriage between a Hindu and a Non-Hindu cannot be solemnised under the Hindu Marriage Act and such a marriage cannot be validated by mere…
summary: The bench of Justice CV Karthikeyan and Justice S Raveekumar thus declared a marriage between a Christian man and a Hindu woman void, holding that the marriage could not.

note.Facts: A Christian man and a Hindu woman were married and later sought validation of their marriage by registration under the Hindu Marriage Act.
note.Issue: Whether a marriage between a Hindu and a non-Hindu can be solemnised or validated under the Hindu Marriage Act merely by registration.
note.Held: The Madras High Court declared the marriage void, holding that such a marriage cannot be solemnised under the Hindu Marriage Act and cannot be validated by registration.
note.Principle: A marriage between a Hindu and a non-Hindu is not permissible under the Hindu Marriage Act and registration does not cure the invalidity.
note.Exam angle: Hindu Marriage Act – question on the requirement of both parties being Hindus (or belonging to religions specified in the Act) and the impossibility of validating an inter-religious marriage through registration.

title: Delhi High Court: Aadhaar Card Not Conclusive Proof of Date of Birth; ESIC Records Prevail in Superannuation Dispute
summary: Delhi High Court: While considering a writ petition challenging the Labour Court’s award holding the termination of a workwoman’s services illegal for non-compliance with Section 25-F , Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (ID Act), a Single Judge Bench of Manoj Kumar Ohri, J. , dismissed the petition, holding that the management had failed to establish that.

note.Facts: A workwoman claimed illegal termination; management argued she had attained superannuation (age 58) on 20 May 2017, relying on her Aadhaar card (DOB 20 May 1959). The Labour Court, using ESIC records (DOB 20 May 1960) furnished by management, held termination illegal for non-compliance with Section 25-F, ID Act.
note.Issue: Whether an Aadhaar card alone can be treated as conclusive proof of date of birth for the purpose of establishing superannuation and the legality of termination under Section 25-F, ID Act.
note.Held: The Delhi High Court dismissed the writ petition, holding that the Aadhaar card is not conclusive proof of date of birth; ESIC records, being earlier and supplied by management, were rightly preferred, and the termination without complying with Section 25-F was illegal.
note.Principle: An Aadhaar card, being based on self-declaration or supporting documents, is not conclusive evidence of date of birth; the party bearing the burden of proof must produce reliable documentary evidence, and a plausible finding based on such evidence cannot be disturbed by a writ court.
note.Provisions: Section 25-F, ID Act; Section 25-G, ID Act; Articles 226 & 227, Constitution of India; UIDAI Office Memorandum (20 Dec 2018); *Saroj v. Iffco-Tokio General Insurance Co.*, 2024 SCC OnLine SC 3038.
note.Exam angle: Industrial Disputes Act – test of superannuation age and compliance with Section 25-F; evidentiary rule that Aadhaar is not conclusive proof of DOB – could be asked as “What evidence is required to establish age for superannuation under ID Act?” or “How does the court treat Aadhaar as proof of DOB?”
